title: Pythagoras
titleEn: The Phoenix, the Fall of Cities, and the Bloodless Table — Metamorphoses XV.335–478
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The speaker brings to an end his argument that nothing keeps the shape it had. He turns first to the earth's own changes — lakes and rivers that alter their powers, an island that once floated and now stands still, Etna that has not always burned and will not burn for ever — and then to creatures generated out of decay or remade in a new shape: bees from a buried bull, a scorpion from a crab's buried remainder, a butterfly from a caterpillar, and the one bird that renews itself, the phoenix, which carries its father's tomb to the temple of Hyperion. From creatures he moves to nations, where Troy, Sparta, Mycenae, Thebes and Athens come down to ruins and names while Dardanian Rome rises, as Helenus foretold to Aeneas in a speech quoted here entire. He closes by drawing the practical conclusion from the passage of souls between bodies: leave animal bodies unharmed, put away nets and snares and baited hooks, and eat no flesh.

sentences.t:
Sic alias aliasque lacus et flumina vires
concipiunt, tempusque fuit, quo navit in undis,
nunc sedet Ortygie.
sentences.l: Thus lakes and rivers take in now one power, now another, and there was a time at which Ortygia swam in the waves; now she sits still.
sentences.i: So lakes and rivers take on one property after another; and there was a time when Ortygia floated on the water — now she stands fast.
sentences.n: *alias aliasque* is “one and then another”, of powers taken on at different times. *tempus fuit, quo* is “there was a time at which”, the relative picking up *tempus*. *Ortygie* is a Greek nominative in -*e*, a name of Delos; *navit* is the perfect of *no*, “swim, float”, set against the present *sedet*.

sentences.t:
Timuit concursibus Argo
undarum sparsas Symplegadas elisarum,
quae nunc inmotae perstant ventisque resistunt.
sentences.l: The Argo feared the Symplegades, sprayed by the collisions of waves crushed between them, which now stand unmoved and resist the winds.
sentences.i: The Argo went in dread of the Symplegades, drenched by the shock of waves squeezed between them — rocks that now stand unmoving and hold out against the winds.
sentences.n: *Argo* is a Greek nominative and *Symplegadas* a Greek accusative plural. *undarum ... elisarum* is a genitive with *concursibus*: the waves are the things crushed, and their clashing is what throws the spray that *sparsas* describes. The relative clause *quae ... perstant* sets present fixity against the past danger.

sentences.t:
Nec, quae sulphureis ardet fornacibus, Aetne
ignea semper erit, neque enim fuit ignea semper.
sentences.l: Nor will Aetna, which burns with sulphurous furnaces, be fiery always; for it was not fiery always either.
sentences.i: Nor will Etna, that blazes with its sulphur furnaces, be fiery for ever — it has not always been fiery either.
sentences.n: *Aetne* is another Greek nominative in -*e*. The relative clause *quae ... ardet* stands between *Nec* and its own antecedent *Aetne*, which Latin word order allows freely. *neque enim* is “for ... not”, giving the ground after the claim; *ignea semper* is repeated in the one line, first with the future *erit*, then with the perfect *fuit*.

sentences.t:
Nam sive est animal tellus et vivit habetque
spiramenta locis flammam exhalantia multis,
spirandi mutare vias, quotiensque movetur,
has finire potest, illas aperire cavernas;
sentences.l: For if on the one hand the earth is a living thing and lives and has breathing-holes that breathe out flame in many places, she can change the ways of breathing, and, as often as she moves, can close these caverns and open those;
sentences.i: For if the earth is an animate thing, alive, with vents that breathe out flame in many places, then she can shift her breathing-passages, and every time she stirs she can shut these caves and open others;
sentences.n: *sive ... sive ... sive* lays out three alternative explanations, at 342, 346 and 350; this is the first. *spirandi* is a genitive gerund with *vias*, “the ways of breathing”. *has ... illas* contrast “these” with “those”, and *cavernas*, held to the last word, serves both.

sentences.t:
sive leves imis venti cohibentur in antris
saxaque cum saxis et habentem semina flammae
materiam iactant, ea concipit ictibus ignem,
antra relinquentur sedatis frigida ventis;
sentences.l: or if light winds are shut up in the deepest caves and hurl rocks against rocks and matter that holds the seeds of flame, and that matter catches fire from the blows, the caves will be left cold when the winds have settled;
sentences.i: or if nimble winds are penned in the deep caverns and dash rock on rock and the stuff that carries the seeds of fire, so that it takes light from the blows, then once the winds die down the caves will be left cold;
sentences.n: The second alternative. *habentem semina flammae materiam* is one phrase, the participle and its object standing in front of the noun *materiam*. *ictibus* is ablative of means, “from the blows”. *sedatis ... ventis* is an ablative absolute, “with the winds settled”, where English wants a clause; it is a construction you will meet constantly.

sentences.t:
sive bitumineae rapiunt incendia vires
luteave exiguis ardescunt sulphura fumis:
sentences.l: or if the powers of bitumen seize the blaze, or yellow sulphur kindles with thin smoke:
sentences.i: or if bitumen's own strength catches fire, or yellow sulphur takes light with a little smoke:
sentences.n: The third alternative. *rapiunt incendia* is “snatch up flames”, of a substance that catches quickly. *-ve* on *lutea* is the enclitic “or”. The colon closes the *sive* series and opens the conclusion.

sentences.t:
nempe ubi terra cibos alimentaque pinguia flammae
non dabit absumptis per longum viribus aevum
naturaeque suum nutrimen deerit edaci,
sentences.l: for assuredly, when the earth will not give the flame food and rich nourishment, its strength used up through a long age, and its own sustenance will fail that devouring nature,
sentences.i: for surely, when the earth no longer gives the flame food and rich nourishment, its strength spent over a long age, and that devouring nature goes without its own sustenance,
sentences.n: *nempe* is “assuredly”, drawing the conclusion the three alternatives share. *ubi* + future indicative makes the time-clause, where English uses a present. *absumptis ... viribus* is a second ablative absolute, interlocked with *per longum ... aevum*: the words of the two phrases alternate within 353. *deerit* is from *desum*, “be lacking”, taking the dative *naturae ... edaci*.

sentences.t: non feret illa famem desertaque deseret ignis.
sentences.l: she will not bear the hunger, and the fire will forsake what has been forsaken.
sentences.i: it will not endure hunger, and the fire will abandon what has already been abandoned.
sentences.n: *illa* is feminine and takes up either *flammae* or *naturae ... edaci* from the lines before; the sense is the same either way. *desertaque deseret* sets a participle of *desero* beside its own future tense: what has been forsaken is what the fire forsakes.

sentences.t:
Esse viros fama est in Hyperborea Pallene,
qui soleant levibus velari corpora plumis,
olim Tritoniacam noviens subiere paludem.
sentences.l: There is a report that there are men in Hyperborean Pallene who are accustomed to be veiled as to their bodies with light feathers; long ago they went nine times beneath the Tritonian marsh.
sentences.i: The story goes that in Hyperborean Pallene there are men whose bodies are regularly covered with soft feathers; long ago they went down nine times beneath the Tritonian marsh.
sentences.n: *fama est* takes an accusative and infinitive, “there is a report that ...”. *velari corpora* is the Greek accusative of respect after a passive, “veiled as to their bodies”; you will meet this often. *subiere* = *subierunt*, the poetic third-plural perfect in -*ere*. Magnus prints *olim*, “long ago”, leaving the dipping as a statement of its own; some editions print *cum*, “when”, which makes the feathers follow the dipping.

sentences.t: Haud equidem credo:
sentences.l: I certainly do not believe it:
sentences.i: For my part, I do not believe it:
sentences.n: *equidem* is the emphatic first person, “I for my part”, and *haud* negates the verb. The colon introduces a second report of the same kind rather than a reason.

sentences.t:
sparsae quoque membra venenis
exercere artes Scythides memorantur easdem.
sentences.l: the Scythian women too, sprinkled as to their limbs with drugs, are recorded to practise the same arts.
sentences.i: Scythian women too, their limbs sprinkled with drugs, are said to work the very same arts.
sentences.n: *membra* is another Greek accusative of respect, this time after the participle *sparsae*, “sprinkled as to their limbs”. *Scythides* is a Greek feminine plural, “Scythian women”. *memorantur* + infinitive is “are said to”. *easdem* stands last in the line, well away from the *artes* it agrees with.

sentences.t:
Siqua fides rebus tamen est addenda probatis,
nonne vides, quaecumque mora fluidoque calore
corpora tabescunt, in parva animalia verti?
sentences.l: If, however, any belief is to be given to things that have been proved, do you not see that whatever bodies rot away with the lapse of time and liquefying heat are turned into small living creatures?
sentences.i: But if proven cases deserve any belief at all — do you not see that any body which decays with time and melting warmth turns into small creatures?
sentences.n: *fides ... est addenda* is a gerundive of obligation; *fidem addere* is the Latin for giving a thing credit, which the literal renders “belief is to be given”. *nonne vides* heads an indirect statement, *corpora ... verti*. *corpora* sits inside the relative clause *quaecumque ... tabescunt* and doubles as the accusative subject of the infinitive. *mora* here is “delay, lapse of time”.

sentences.t:
I quoque, delectos mactatos obrue tauros
(cognita res usu) de putri viscere passim
florilegae nascuntur apes,
sentences.l: Go, you too: bury bulls picked out and slaughtered (the thing is known by experience) — from the rotten flesh, all over it, flower-gathering bees are born,
sentences.i: Go and do it yourself: bury bulls, chosen and slaughtered — experience has taught the thing — and out of the putrid flesh, all over it, bees that gather from flowers are born,
sentences.n: *I* is the imperative of *eo*, “go”, and *quoque* is the adverb “also”, not *quo-que*. *delectos mactatos* stacks two participles on *tauros* with no connective between them. *cognita res usu* is a parenthesis in the nominative, standing outside the sentence's grammar. Magnus prints *I quoque, delectos*; some editions print *in scrobe deiecto*, “in a pit, once he is thrown down”, which removes the imperative.

sentences.t:
quae more parentum
rura colunt operique favent in spemque laborant;
sentences.l: which in the manner of their parents work the fields and attend to their task and labour toward a hope;
sentences.i: and like their parents they work the land, keep at the task, and labour for what is to come;
sentences.n: *quae* is the relative on *apes*, “and they”. *more parentum* is ablative of manner. *favent* takes the dative *operi*, “are devoted to the work”. *in spem laborant* is “labour towards a hope”, of work done for a future yield.

sentences.t: pressus humo bellator equus crabronis origo est;
sentences.l: a war-horse pressed under the earth is the origin of the hornet;
sentences.i: a warhorse buried in the ground is where the hornet comes from;
sentences.n: *pressus humo* is “pressed down under the earth”, the bare ablative doing the work of “buried”. *bellator* is a noun used adjectivally with *equus*, “a warrior horse”. *origo est* takes the genitive *crabronis*.

sentences.l: if you should take the hollow claws away from a shore-crab, and put the rest under the earth, from the buried part a scorpion will come out and will threaten with its hooked tail;
sentences.i: take the hollow claws off a shore crab and set the rest under the ground: out of the buried part a scorpion will emerge and threaten with its hooked tail;
sentences.n: *demas* and *supponas* are present subjunctives in the protasis, “if you should take away ... should place”, with future indicatives answering them. *cancro* is a dative of separation with *demas*, and *terrae* a dative with *supponas*. *unca* agrees with *cauda* across the intervening verb.

sentences.t:
quaeque solent canis frondes intexere filis
agrestes tineae (res observata colonis)
ferali mutant cum papilione figuram.
sentences.l: and the field caterpillars which are accustomed to weave leaves over with grey threads (a thing observed by farmers) exchange their shape with the funereal butterfly.
sentences.i: and the field caterpillars that spin their grey threads across the leaves — farmers have watched it happen — exchange their shape for that of the funereal butterfly.
sentences.n: The relative clause *quaeque ... intexere filis* comes before its noun *agrestes tineae*. *mutare aliquid cum aliquo* is “exchange one thing for another”, so the shape is swapped for the butterfly's. *res observata colonis* is a second parenthesis in the nominative, with a dative of agent, “a thing observed by farmers”. *ferali* means “of the dead, funereal”; why the butterfly earns the word is not explained here.

sentences.t:
Semina limus habet virides generantia ranas,
et generat truncas pedibus, mox apta natando
cura dat, utque eadem sint longis saltibus apta,
posterior superat partes mensura priores.
sentences.l: The mud holds seeds that engender green frogs, and it engenders them cut short as to their feet; soon its care gives them what is fit for swimming, and, so that the same may be fit for long leaps as well, the hinder measure outdoes the parts in front.
sentences.i: The mud holds the seeds that breed green frogs, and breeds them docked of feet; then its care supplies what is fit for swimming, and so that the same limbs may serve for long jumps, the hind pair is made to outdo the front.
sentences.n: *truncas pedibus* is “cut short in respect of feet”, an ablative of respect. *apta natando* is a neuter plural with a dative gerund, “things fit for swimming”. *utque ... sint* is a purpose clause. *partes ... priores* is split around *mensura*. Magnus prints *cura*, making nature's care the giver; some editions print *crura*, “legs”, as the thing given.

sentences.t:
Nec catulus, partu quem reddidit ursa recenti,
sed male viva caro est:
sentences.l: The cub which the she-bear has brought forth in a recent birth is not a cub, but flesh scarcely alive:
sentences.i: What the she-bear has just brought forth is no cub, but barely living flesh:
sentences.n: *Nec ... sed* is “not ... but”, the negative attached to the noun while one *est* serves both halves. *partu ... recenti* straddles the relative clause *quem reddidit ursa*. *male viva* is “scarcely alive”, *male* weakening rather than negating.

sentences.t:
lambendo mater in artus
fingit et in formam, quantam capit ipsa, reducit.
sentences.l: by licking, the mother shapes it into limbs and brings it back into a form as great as she herself holds.
sentences.i: by licking, the mother moulds it into limbs and draws it into a shape as large as her own.
sentences.n: *lambendo* is an ablative gerund of means, “by licking”. *in artus fingit* and *in formam ... reducit* both use *in* with the accusative of the result reached. *quantam capit ipsa* is “as great as she herself contains”: the mother's own size sets the limit.

sentences.t:
Nonne vides, quos cera tegit sexangula, fetus
melliferarum apium sine membris corpora nasci
et serosque pedes serasque adsumere pennas?
sentences.l: Do you not see that the young of the honey-bearing bees, which the six-cornered wax covers, are born as bodies without limbs, and take on late feet and late wings?
sentences.i: Do you not see that the grubs of the honey-making bees, sealed under the six-cornered wax, are born as bodies with no limbs, and only later take on feet and wings?
sentences.n: *Nonne vides* again heads an indirect statement, with *fetus* the accusative subject of both *nasci* and *adsumere*. The relative clause *quos cera tegit sexangula* stands inside the accusative phrase, before its own noun *fetus*. *seros ... seras* is doubled for emphasis, “late ... late”.

sentences.t:
Iunonis volucrem, quae cauda sidera portat,
armigerumque Iovis Cythereiadasque columbas
et genus omne avium mediis e partibus ovi,
ni sciret fieri, quis nasci posse putaret?
sentences.l: Juno's bird, which carries stars in its tail, and the armour-bearer of Jupiter, and the Cytherean doves, and the whole race of birds — who would suppose that they could be born out of the middle parts of an egg, if he did not know that it happens?
sentences.i: Juno's bird with the stars in its tail, Jupiter's armour-bearer, Venus's doves, and every kind of bird besides — who would think they could be born from the inside of an egg, if he did not know that it happens?
sentences.n: Four accusatives are held at the front through three lines before the verb *putaret* arrives as the last word. They are the subjects of *posse nasci* in the indirect statement. *ni sciret* is “if he did not know”, an unreal condition answered by *putaret*. *armigerum Iovis* is the eagle; *Iunonis volucrem*, named by the stars in its tail, the peacock. *Cythereiadas* is “of Cythera”, the island that gives Venus one of her names, which is why the idiomatic says “Venus's”.

sentences.t:
Sunt qui, cum clauso putrefacta est spina sepulcro,
mutari credant humanas angue medullas.
sentences.l: There are those who believe that, when the spine has rotted in the closed tomb, human marrow is exchanged for a snake.
sentences.i: Some believe that when the spine has decayed in the sealed tomb, a man's marrow turns into a snake.
sentences.n: *Sunt qui ... credant* takes the subjunctive, “there are people of the sort who believe”. *mutari* with the bare ablative *angue* is “be exchanged for a snake” — the same idea as *mutant cum papilione* at 374, but without the preposition. *clauso ... sepulcro* wraps itself round *putrefacta est spina*.

sentences.t: Haec tamen ex aliis generis primordia ducunt:
sentences.l: These, however, draw the first beginnings of their kind from other things:
sentences.i: All these, though, take the origin of their kind from something else:
sentences.n: *Haec* is neuter plural, gathering up the creatures just listed. *generis primordia* is “the first beginnings of a kind”, the object of *ducunt*, with *ex aliis* the source. The colon opens the contrast.

sentences.t: una est, quae reparet seque ipsa reseminet, ales.
sentences.l: there is one bird which restores itself and re-sows itself.
sentences.i: there is a single bird that renews itself and sows itself afresh.
sentences.n: *quae reparet ... reseminet* is a relative clause of characteristic, hence the subjunctives: “the sort of bird that renews itself”. *una ... ales* is split around that whole clause, *ales* arriving as the last word. *se* is object of both verbs; *ipsa* is nominative and strengthens the subject, not the object — the bird does the renewing itself, with nothing else involved.

sentences.t:
Assyrii phoenica vocant; non fruge neque herbis,
sed turis lacrimis et suco vivit amomi.
sentences.l: The Assyrians call it the phoenix; it lives not on grain nor on grasses, but on the tears of frankincense and the juice of amomum.
sentences.i: The Assyrians call it the phoenix; it feeds not on grain or herbage but on the tears of frankincense and the sap of amomum.
sentences.n: *phoenica* is a Greek accusative singular. *vivit* with the ablative is “live on, live by”. *turis lacrimis* are the drops of resin that ooze from the incense tree, called its tears. *amomi* is a genitive with *suco*, held to the end of the line. *amomum* is an eastern aromatic shrub; both layers keep the name rather than substituting a familiar plant.

sentences.t:
Haec ubi quinque suae complevit saecula vitae,
ilicis in ramis tremulaeque cacumine palmae
unguibus et puro nidum sibi construit ore.
sentences.l: When this bird has completed five ages of its own life, on the branches of a holm-oak and at the top of a trembling palm it builds itself a nest with its claws and clean beak.
sentences.i: When it has filled out five ages of its own life, it builds itself a nest in the branches of a holm-oak, at the crown of a swaying palm, with its talons and unpolluted beak.
sentences.n: *Haec* is feminine, of the bird. *ubi* with the perfect indicative is “when once it has”. *suae ... vitae* is a genitive split around *complevit saecula*. *puro ... ore* is “with a clean mouth”, in keeping with the diet just described.

sentences.t:
Quo simul ac casias et nardi lenis aristas
quassaque cum fulva substravit cinnama murra,
se super imponit finitque in odoribus aevum.
sentences.l: As soon as it has strewn in it cassia and the ears of smooth nard and crushed cinnamon with tawny myrrh, it lays itself on top and ends its lifetime among the perfumes.
sentences.i: As soon as it has laid down there cassia, spikes of soft nard, crushed cinnamon and yellow myrrh, it settles itself on top and finishes its life among the scents.
sentences.n: *Quo* is a connecting relative, “and in it”, taking up the nest of the line before; a sentence opening with a relative like this is best read as “and it”. *simul ac* with the perfect is “as soon as”. *substravit* is “has spread underneath”, hence the pile the bird then lies on; in *se super imponit*, *super* is an adverb, “on top”. *aevum* here is a lifetime, not an age of the world.

sentences.t:
Inde ferunt, totidem qui vivere debeat annos,
corpore de patrio parvum phoenica renasci.
sentences.l: From there they report that a small phoenix, one which is to live just as many years, is born again out of its father's body.
sentences.i: From it, they say, a small phoenix is born again out of its parent's body, to live out just as many years.
sentences.n: *ferunt* takes an accusative and infinitive, “they report that ...”. *qui ... debeat* is a relative clause of characteristic, standing before its noun *phoenica*. *corpore de patrio* puts the preposition between adjective and noun, which verse allows freely. *patrio* is literally “of the father”, which the literal keeps, though the bird has been feminine throughout (*una ... ales* at 392, *Haec* at 395); “of the parent” is the force, and the idiomatic takes it.

sentences.t:
Cum dedit huic aetas vires, onerique ferendo est,
ponderibus nidi ramos levat arboris altae
fertque pius cunasque suas patriumque sepulcrum,
sentences.l: When age has given it strength, and it is fit for carrying the load, it lifts the branches of the tall tree free of the nest's weights and dutifully carries both its own cradle and its father's tomb,
sentences.i: When age has given it strength and it is equal to the load, it relieves the tall tree's branches of the nest's weight and dutifully carries what is at once its own cradle and its father's tomb,
sentences.n: *oneri ferendo est* is the dative gerundive of fitness, “is up to the carrying of the load”. *levat ... ponderibus* is “lightens the branches of the weights”, an ablative of separation. *pius* does adverbial work, and is the word for duty owed to a parent. *cunas ... sepulcrum* name one and the same object.

sentences.t:
perque leves auras Hyperionis urbe potitus
ante fores sacras Hyperionis aede reponit.
sentences.l: and, having gained the city of Hyperion through the light airs, it lays it down before the sacred doors in Hyperion's temple.
sentences.i: and through the light air it reaches the city of Hyperion and sets it down before the sacred doors, inside his temple.
sentences.n: *potitus* is the perfect participle of the deponent *potior* and takes the ablative *urbe*, “having gained the city”. *Hyperionis* stands in both lines, first of the city and then of the temple; the name is the Sun's. *aede* is an ablative of place with no preposition, normal in verse.

sentences.l: If, however, there is anything of strange novelty in those things, let us wonder that the hyena alternates its turns, and that the one which, lately a female, endured the male at her back is now itself a male;
sentences.i: But if there is anything strangely new in those cases, let us rather wonder at the hyena's alternating turns — that the creature which lately, as a female, submitted to the male at her back is now a male itself;
sentences.n: *miremur* is a hortatory subjunctive, “let us wonder”, governing two accusative-and-infinitive clauses. *alternare vices* is “to alternate turns”. The relative clause *quae modo femina ... passa marem est* has no antecedent before it: *hyaenam* arrives only as the last word of the sentence. *modo*, “just now”, is set against *nunc*.

sentences.t:
id quoque, quod ventis animal nutritur et aura,
protinus adsimulat, tetigit quoscumque colores.
sentences.l: that creature too, which is fed on winds and air, at once imitates whatever colours it has touched.
sentences.i: and that animal too, the one nourished on wind and air, instantly copies whatever colours it has touched.
sentences.n: *id ... animal* is split, the noun *animal* standing inside its own relative clause while *id* stays outside it. *ventis ... et aura* is ablative of means with the passive *nutritur*. *quoscumque colores* is the object of *tetigit* inside the relative clause and of *adsimulat* outside it, and the whole clause follows *adsimulat*. *quoque* here is the adverb “also”, not *quo-que*, “and with which” — a trap worth watching for.

sentences.t: Victa racemifero lyncas dedit India Baccho:
sentences.l: Conquered India gave lynxes to cluster-bearing Bacchus:
sentences.i: India, once conquered, gave lynxes to Bacchus of the grape clusters:
sentences.n: *Victa* stands at the head of the line, three words away from the *India* it agrees with. *racemifero* is a compound adjective, “bearing grape-clusters”, in the dative with *dedit*. The colon opens the marvel the lynxes furnish.

sentences.t:
e quibus, ut memorant, quidquid vesica remisit,
vertitur in lapides et congelat aere tacto.
sentences.l: from which, as they relate, whatever the bladder has let go is turned into stones and hardens when the air has been touched.
sentences.i: from them, so people tell it, whatever the bladder releases turns to stone and sets hard the moment it meets the air.
sentences.n: *e quibus* is a connecting relative on the lynxes. *ut memorant* is a parenthesis, “as they tell it” — the speaker reports the marvel without vouching for it, as he refused to vouch at 359. *aere tacto* is an ablative absolute, “the air having been touched”, i.e. on contact with the air.

sentences.t:
Sic et curalium quo primum contigit auras
tempore, durescit:
sentences.l: So too coral hardens at the time at which it first touched the air:
sentences.i: So too coral turns hard at the very moment it first meets the air:
sentences.n: *quo ... tempore* is a relative clause with its antecedent *tempore* inside it and split across the line-end; the demonstrative “at that time” is left to be supplied. *curalium* is a neuter noun, the subject of *durescit*. *auras* is a plural for the single element, air.

sentences.t: mollis fuit herba sub undis.
sentences.l: it was a soft plant under the waves.
sentences.i: under the water it had been a soft plant.
sentences.n: The clause is set beside the last with no connective, a bare contrast: hard once it touches the air, soft while it is in the sea. *herba* is a predicate noun with *fuit*.

sentences.t:
Desinet ante dies et in alto Phoebus anhelos
aequore tinget equos, quam consequar omnia verbis
in species translata novas:
sentences.l: The day will end sooner, and Phoebus will dip his panting horses in the deep sea, than I shall run through in words all the things carried over into new shapes:
sentences.i: Daylight will give out, and Phoebus will plunge his panting horses into the deep, before I can tell over in words everything that has passed into new forms:
sentences.n: *ante ... quam* is split across two lines, “sooner ... than”, with *consequar* following it. *in alto ... aequore* is an ablative of place wrapped around *Phoebus anhelos*. *translata* is the participle of *transfero*, “carried across”, agreeing with *omnia*; *in species ... novas* gives the goal of the carrying.

sentences.t:
sic tempora verti
cernimus atque illas adsumere robora gentes,
concidere has.
sentences.l: thus we see that the times are turned about, and that those nations take on strength, these collapse.
sentences.i: in just this way we watch the ages turn, and see one people gather strength while another falls in.
sentences.n: *cernimus* heads an indirect statement with three infinitives: *verti*, *adsumere*, *concidere*. *tempora verti* is passive, “that the times are turned”; the literal keeps the passive and the idiomatic lets English turn it round. *illas ... has* are “those ... these”, the second left without a noun of its own.

sentences.t:
Sic magna fuit censuque virisque
perque decem potuit tantum dare sanguinis annos,
nunc humilis veteres tantummodo Troia ruinas
et pro divitiis tumulos ostendit avorum.
sentences.l: So she was great both in wealth and in men, and through ten years could give so much blood; now, humbled, Troy shows only her old ruins and, in place of riches, the burial mounds of her forefathers.
sentences.i: So Troy was great in wealth and in men, and for ten years could pour out so much blood; now, brought low, she has nothing to show but her old ruins and, instead of riches, the graves of her ancestors.
sentences.n: *Troia* is the subject of the whole sentence but is not named until its third line, after *fuit* and *potuit* have already agreed with her. *censu ... virisque* is an ablative of respect, “in wealth and in men”. *tantum ... sanguinis* is a partitive genitive, “so much of blood”. *pro divitiis* is “in place of riches”.

sentences.t:
Clara fuit Sparte, magnae viguere Mycenae,
nec non et Cecropis nec non Amphionis arces.
sentences.l: Sparta was famous, great Mycenae flourished, and so too the citadels of Cecrops and of Amphion.
sentences.i: Sparta was renowned, mighty Mycenae was in its prime, and so were the strongholds of Cecrops and of Amphion.
sentences.n: *viguere* = *viguerunt*, the poetic perfect in -*ere* again. *Sparte* is a Greek nominative in -*e*. *nec non ... nec non* is a double negative used as a strong “and also”, and is repeated. *arces* serves both genitives: the cities are named by a legendary king or builder rather than by their own names.

sentences.t:
Vile solum Sparte est, altae cecidere Mycenae,
Oedipodioniae quid sunt, nisi nomina, Thebae?
sentences.l: Sparta is cheap ground, lofty Mycenae has fallen; what are the Thebes of Oedipus, if not names?
sentences.i: Sparta is worthless soil now, high Mycenae has come down — and Oedipus's Thebes, what is it but a name?
sentences.n: *cecidere* = *ceciderunt*, the -*ere* perfect once more. *Mycenae* and *Thebae* are plural in form in Latin and take plural verbs and predicates — hence *cecidere* and the plural *nomina* — where English treats each city as one. *Oedipodioniae* is a Greek adjective built on Oedipus's name. *Vile solum* is the predicate: the city is now merely cheap ground.

sentences.t: Quid Pandioniae restant, nisi nomen, Athenae?
sentences.l: What do Pandion's Athens remain, if not a name?
sentences.i: And what is left of Pandion's Athens but a name?
sentences.n: *quid* is an internal accusative with *restant*, “remain as what?”, answering *quid sunt* in the line before. *Pandioniae* is another adjective built on the name of a legendary Athenian king. *nomen* is singular here where 429 had the plural *nomina*, though *Athenae* is as plural in form as *Thebae*.

sentences.t:
Nunc quoque Dardaniam fama est consurgere Romam,
Appenninigenae quae proxima Thybridis undis
mole sub ingenti rerum fundamina ponit:
sentences.l: Now too there is a report that Dardanian Rome is rising, which, closest to the waters of the Apennine-born Tiber, lays the foundations of a state under a vast mass:
sentences.i: Now too the word is that Dardanian Rome is rising — she who, hard by the waters of the Apennine-born Tiber, is laying the foundations of a state beneath a vast weight of building:
sentences.n: *fama est* takes an accusative and infinitive again, *Romam consurgere*. *proxima* governs the dative *undis*. *Appenninigenae* is a compound adjective, “born of the Apennines”, agreeing with *Thybridis*, the Greek genitive of the river's name. *rerum fundamina* is “the foundations of a state”, *res* in its political sense.

sentences.t:
haec igitur formam crescendo mutat et olim
immensi caput orbis erit.
sentences.l: she therefore changes her shape by growing, and one day will be the head of a measureless world.
sentences.i: so she changes her form as she grows, and one day will be the head of a boundless world.
sentences.n: *crescendo* is an ablative gerund of means, “by growing”. *haec* is the connecting demonstrative, taking up *Romam* from 431. *olim* looks forward here, “one day”, where at 358 the same word looked back, “long ago”. *caput* is the predicate noun with *erit*.

sentences.t:
Sic dicere vates
faticinasque ferunt sortes quantumque recordor,
dixerat Aeneae, cum res Troiana labaret,
Priamides Helenus flenti dubioque salutis:
sentences.l: So the seers and the fate-telling oracles say, they report; and, as far as I recall, Helenus son of Priam had said to Aeneas, weeping and doubtful of his safety, when the Trojan state was tottering:
sentences.i: So the prophets and the fate-speaking oracles declare, they say; and, so far as I remember, Priam's son Helenus had said this to Aeneas as he wept, despairing of rescue, when Troy's fortunes were giving way:
sentences.n: *ferunt* takes an accusative and infinitive: *vates ... sortes* are the subjects of *dicere*. *quantum recordor* is “as far as I remember”, the speaker vouching only for his memory. *flenti dubioque* are datives agreeing with *Aeneae*, and *salutis* is a genitive after *dubio*, “doubtful of his safety”. *cum ... labaret* is a *cum* clause with the subjunctive. The colon opens the quoted speech.

sentences.t:
“Nate dea, si nota satis praesagia nostrae
mentis habes, non tota cadet te sospite Troia!
sentences.l: “Son of a goddess, if you hold well enough known the forebodings of my mind, Troy will not fall entire while you are safe!
sentences.i: “Goddess-born, if you know the forecasts of my mind well enough, Troy will not fall whole while you survive!
sentences.n: *Nate dea* is a vocative with an ablative of origin, “born from a goddess”. *nota ... habes* is “you have them known”, that is, you know them. *nostrae mentis* is a plural for the singular, “my mind”. *te sospite* is an ablative absolute made of a pronoun and an adjective, with no participle at all: “with you safe”.

sentences.t: Flamma tibi ferrumque dabunt iter:
sentences.l: Flame and iron will give you a road:
sentences.i: Fire and the sword will open a way for you:
sentences.n: *dabunt iter* is “will give a passage”: the fire and the sword are the means of escape here, not the thing barring it. *tibi* is a dative of advantage. The colon opens the explanation.

sentences.t:
ibis et una
Pergama rapta feres, donec Troiaeque tibique
externum patrio contingat amicius arvum.
sentences.l: you will go, and together with you will carry Pergamum snatched away, until a foreign field falls to Troy and to you, one friendlier than your father's.
sentences.i: you will go, and carry Pergamum away with you, until a foreign land comes to Troy and to you, kinder than the land of your fathers.
sentences.n: *una* is the adverb “together”, not the numeral. *Pergama* is a Greek neuter plural, the citadel of Troy, with *rapta* agreeing. *donec ... contingat* takes the subjunctive of an event still looked for. *patrio* is an ablative of comparison after *amicius*, which agrees with *arvum* at the end of the line.

sentences.t:
Urbem etiam cerno Phrygios debere nepotes,
quanta nec est nec erit nec visa prioribus annis.
sentences.l: I see besides that Phrygian descendants are bound to raise a city, one as great as none is, nor will be, nor was seen in earlier years.
sentences.i: I see too that Phrygian descendants are destined to raise a city as great as none that is, none that will be, and none seen in earlier ages.
sentences.n: *Urbem* stands first, before the verb of seeing. *cerno* takes an accusative and infinitive, of prophetic sight. *debere* with the accusative *Urbem* is literally “to owe a city”, of a thing destiny requires of them; the literal turns it to “are bound to raise”, which is its force here. *quanta* is the correlative of size, “as great as”, answered by the three negatives *nec ... nec ... nec*; *visa* has *est* supplied from the first of them.

sentences.l: Other chieftains will make her powerful through long ages, but one born from the blood of Iulus will make her mistress of the world;
sentences.i: Other leading men will make her powerful through long ages, but a man born of Iulus's blood will make her mistress of the world;
sentences.n: One verb, the singular *efficiet*, serves two subjects: a plural has to be supplied for *alii proceres*. *hanc ... potentem* and *dominam rerum* are the two predicate accusatives it governs. *de sanguine natus Iuli* is “born from the blood of Iulus”, with the genitive held to the end of its line.

sentences.t:
quo cum tellus erit usa, fruentur
aetheriae sedes, caelumque erit exitus illi.”
sentences.l: and when the earth has made use of him, the heavenly seats will enjoy him, and heaven will be his going-out.”
sentences.i: and when earth has had the use of him, the courts of heaven will have the enjoyment of him, and the sky will be his journey's end.”
sentences.n: *quo* is a connecting relative in the ablative with *utor*: *erit usa* is the future perfect of that deponent, “will have made use of”. *fruentur* likewise takes an ablative, understood from *quo*. *exitus* is a way out, the end of a road, with *illi* the dative of the person. The closing quotation mark ends the speech opened at 439.

sentences.t:
Haec Helenum cecinisse penatigero Aeneae
mente memor refero, cognataque moenia laetor
crescere et utiliter Phrygibus vicisse Pelasgos.
sentences.l: That Helenus sang these things to Aeneas the bearer of the household gods I report, remembering it in my mind; and I rejoice that kindred walls are growing and that the Pelasgians conquered to the Phrygians' profit.
sentences.i: I report from memory that Helenus prophesied this to Aeneas as he carried his household gods; and I am glad that walls of my own kin are rising, and that the Greeks won to the Trojans' benefit.
sentences.n: *Haec ... cecinisse* is an accusative and infinitive after *refero*; *cano* is used of prophecy, “sang, foretold”. *penatigero* is a compound adjective, “carrying the household gods”, dative with *Aeneae*. *laetor* governs two further infinitives, *crescere* and *vicisse*. *utiliter Phrygibus* is “usefully for the Phrygians”, a dative with the adverb. Whose kin *cognata* means is not said here.

sentences.t:
Ne tamen oblitis ad metam tendere longe
exspatiemur equis, caelum et quodcumque sub illo est,
inmutat formas tellusque et quidquid in illa est:
sentences.l: But so that we may not stray far off, our horses having forgotten to make for the turning-post: the sky and whatever is beneath it changes its forms, and the earth too and whatever is in it:
sentences.i: But so that we do not run wide of the course, our horses forgetting to head for the post — the sky and all beneath it alters its forms, and so do the earth and all within it:
sentences.n: *Ne ... exspatiemur* is a negative purpose clause, “so that we may not stray”. *oblitis ... equis* is ablative: *obliviscor* is deponent, so the participle is active in force and takes the infinitive *tendere* as its object. The image is a chariot running wide of the turning-post. *inmutat* is singular although several subjects stand with it. *quodcumque* and *quidquid* pair the sky's contents with the earth's.

sentences.t:
nos quoque, pars mundi, quoniam non corpora solum,
verum etiam volucres animae sumus inque ferinas
possumus ire domos pecudumque in corpora condi,
sentences.l: we too, a part of the world, since we are not bodies only but winged souls as well, and can go into the homes of wild beasts and be stowed away in the bodies of cattle —
sentences.i: we too are a part of the world; and since we are not bodies alone but souls that fly, able to enter the dwellings of wild beasts and be shut up in the bodies of cattle —
sentences.n: *nos quoque* is the subject of *sinamus*, which does not arrive until the sixth line of the sentence, at 461; everything here is the *quoniam* clause giving the reason. *volucres animae* is “winged souls”, a predicate with *sumus*. *ferinas ... domos* are “the houses of wild beasts”, meaning their bodies. *condi* is a passive infinitive, “be stowed away”.

sentences.t:
corpora, quae possunt animas habuisse parentum
aut fratrum aut aliquo iunctorum foedere nobis
aut hominum certe, tuta esse et honesta sinamus
neve Thyesteis cumulemus viscera mensis!
sentences.l: let us allow the bodies which may have held the souls of our parents, or of our brothers, or of people joined to us by some bond, or of human beings at the least, to be safe and unviolated, and let us not heap our own flesh with Thyestean tables!
sentences.i: let us leave unharmed and undishonoured the bodies that may have held the souls of our parents, or our brothers, or of people bound to us by some tie, or at the very least of human beings — and let us not load our own flesh with the feast of Thyestes!
sentences.n: *sinamus* is a hortatory subjunctive taking an accusative and infinitive, *corpora ... tuta esse et honesta*. *possunt habuisse* is “are able to have held”, a possibility about the past. *aliquo ... foedere* is ablative with *iunctorum*. *honesta* here is “unviolated, treated with respect”, not “honest”. *Thyesteis ... mensis* is ablative with *cumulemus*: the banquet of Thyestes, at which a man was served the flesh of his own children.

sentences.t:
Quam male consuescit, quam se parat ille cruori
impius humano, vituli qui guttura cultro
rumpit et inmotas praebet mugitibus aures,
sentences.l: How badly he grows used to it, how he readies himself for human blood, that impious man, who bursts open the throat of a calf with a knife and offers unmoved ears to its bellowing,
sentences.i: What a bad habit he is forming, how he is making himself ready for human blood — that godless man who rips open a calf's throat with the knife and keeps his ears unmoved at its bellowing,
sentences.n: *Quam ... quam* is exclamatory, “how badly ... how much”. *cruori humano* is dative with *se parat*, “makes himself ready for”. *impius* is the word for a breach of duty owed to gods and kin; it opens 464, a line away from the *ille* it agrees with, which stands second from last in 463. *guttura* is a poetic plural for one throat, and *inmotas* is predicative with *aures*: the ears stay unmoved.

sentences.t:
aut qui vagitus similes puerilibus haedum
edentem iugulare potest, aut alite vesci,
cui dedit ipse cibos!
sentences.l: or who can cut the throat of a kid that utters cries like those of children, or feed on a bird to which he himself gave food!
sentences.i: or who can slit the throat of a kid as it makes cries like a baby's, or eat the bird he fed with his own hand!
sentences.n: *vagitus similes puerilibus* is “wailings like those of children”, *similis* with a dative and *vagitibus* understood with *puerilibus*. *edentem* is from *edo*, “utter, put forth”, agreeing with *haedum* — not the other *edo*, “eat”. *vesci* takes the ablative *alite*. *ipse* in the relative clause points the charge back at the man.

sentences.t:
Quantum est, quod desit in istis
ad plenum facinus?
sentences.l: How much is there that is wanting, in those doings, towards a full crime?
sentences.i: How much is still lacking in those practices of yours to make the crime complete?
sentences.n: *Quantum est, quod desit* is “how much is there that is wanting”, with *desit* subjunctive in a relative clause of characteristic. *ad plenum facinus* is “towards a complete crime”, the mark these deeds fall short of. *istis* is the contemptuous demonstrative, “those of yours”.

sentences.t: Quo transitus inde paratur?
sentences.l: To what point is the passage from there being prepared?
sentences.i: And where does the crossing being made ready from there run to?
sentences.n: *Quo* is the interrogative of motion, “to what point”. *transitus* is a crossing-over, from one kind of killing to the next; the answer the question expects was named at 463–464, human blood. *paratur* is passive, with no agent given.

sentences.t:
Bos aret aut mortem senioribus imputet annis,
horriferum contra borean ovis arma ministret,
ubera dent saturae manibus pressanda capellae!
sentences.l: Let the ox plough, or charge its death to its older years; let the sheep supply armour against the shudder-bringing north wind; let well-fed she-goats give udders to be pressed by hands!
sentences.i: Let the ox plough, or lay its death to the account of old age; let the sheep furnish armour against the north wind that makes men shudder; let full-fed she-goats offer udders for the hand to press!
sentences.n: Four jussive subjunctives, *aret*, *imputet*, *ministret*, *dent*: “let it ...”. *mortem ... imputet annis* is a book-keeping metaphor, charging the death to the years' account. *arma* is “defensive gear”, here the fleece. *pressanda* is a gerundive with *ubera*, “udders to be pressed”; *saturae* agrees with *capellae*.

sentences.t:
Retia cum pedicis laqueosque artesque dolosas
tollite nec volucrem viscata fallite virga,
sentences.l: Take away nets along with snares and nooses and crafty devices, and do not deceive the bird with a limed rod,
sentences.i: Do away with nets, snares, nooses and cunning contrivances, and do not trick the bird with a limed twig,
sentences.n: *tollite* and *fallite* are plural imperatives: the address widens from the single man of the lines before, who was *ille ... qui*, to a whole audience. *cum pedicis* is “along with snares”, the preposition joining rather than instrumental. *viscata ... virga* is an ablative of means, a rod smeared with birdlime, split around *fallite*.

sentences.t:
nec formidatis cervos includite pennis,
nec celate cibis uncos fallacibus hamos!
sentences.l: nor pen deer in with dreaded feathers, nor hide hooked barbs in deceiving food!
sentences.i: nor fence deer in with the feathers they dread, nor hide the barbed hooks in treacherous bait!
sentences.n: *nec ... nec* carries on the plural imperatives. *formidatis ... pennis* is an ablative of means: feathered cords strung up to drive game towards the nets; *formidatis* is the participle, “feared”. *uncos ... hamos* and *cibis ... fallacibus* interlock, each pair split around a word of the other.

sentences.t:
Perdite, siqua nocent, verum haec quoque perdite tantum:
ora vacent epulis alimentaque mitia carpant!”
sentences.l: Destroy them, if any do harm; but even these, destroy only: let mouths be free of such feasts and gather gentle nourishment!”
sentences.i: Kill them, if any do harm — but even these, only kill: let your mouths keep clear of such meals and take mild food instead!”
sentences.n: *siqua nocent* is “if any do harm”, *si qua* printed as one word by the edition. *tantum* is the adverb “only”, limiting *perdite*: kill, but do not eat. *ora vacent* is a jussive subjunctive with an ablative of separation, “let mouths be empty of”. Magnus prints *epulis*, “of the feasts”; some editions print *cruore*, “of blood”, which changes what the mouth is to be kept clear of. The closing quotation mark ends a speech whose opening lies before these lines: nothing in this part opens it.
